SB 83 Local Choice Energy Act, is scheduled in Senate Tax, Business, and Transportation Committee TOMORROW, Tuesday 3/9 starting around 1:30pm. Local Choice Energy opens up New Mexico's electricity markets to competition and puts local communities in control of who supplies their energy. It would allow any local community to pool their electricity demand and create a local utility, who works with the investor owned utility in the service area to transmit and distribute that electricity. NM has two investor-owned (IOU) monopolies and a majority of residents in NM are forced to use PNM and El Paso electric even though we'd rather not pay for their gas, coal, or nuclear energy portfolios. The bill would make it legal for communities and Tribal Nations to create utilities and decide where our energy comes from, produce our own energy, and keep energy dollars circulating in our local and state economies instead of shipping energy profits off to Wall Street.

"9-point financial plan for recovery"
My 9-point plan for recovery is to end the need for an "emergency levy" and solve our school district's financial crisis once and for all. 

Here is a starting point for discussion to retore sound conservative principles to restore frugal financial management to our schools.

The schools are our most expensive property tax burden. It is time that someone starts looking at the money. Much of this analysis comes from past audits, which board members ignored. 

1. The school board has a little known, but costly perk. The school board not only pays the employer's share of the benefits, but the bonus is, they will also pay the employee share. It's called a "pickup." 

Employees love it as the "pickups" benefits themselves are very rich, and the cost is zero to the employee. 

The state auditor said this was short term thinking that leads to a severe financial taxpayer burden. In short, it is a "hidden taxpayer rip-off" and needs to end.

2. Benefit plans should be in line with the private sector. Total cost per employee should including account for wages and benefits combined to arrive at a correct taxpayer cost. 

No matter the position, every hired employee should have a total cost sheet so school board members can make well informed financial decisions. Total cost per employee should also state any projected bonuses.

3. Unlimited sick days sound great, but sick day banking days become abusive and wreak havoc on liability obligations. By putting limits on sick days like the private sector is a far more financially responsible path.

4. All bonus payments need to end until a complete forensic audit evaluates the bonuses from a business-oriented perspective. Perks paid out as a method of inflating wages is an indirect manner to hide the real cost from taxpayers and needs to cease. 

5. All additional educational compensation reimbursements need to be approved and have to be "State required" to perform the position currently held. If the current job does not require other educational benefits, the employee should pick that expense up, not the employer.

6. End the practice of double-dipping during hiring. It is ultimately more expensive to the taxpayers and is a bad deal. Once retired, never rehired.

7. Reform salary schedules and step systems to reflect the communities willing to tax themselves. Overly aggressive payroll schedules need to be reviewed and adjusted to reflect the economy and private sector. Right now, the current system is a bad deal for taxpayers. We need a fair deal, not a bad deal. A "top out" wage rate requires implementation.  

8. Stop paying bonuses to employees as a reward for retiring.

9. Produce benefit summary sheets for the taxpayer to examine average retirement savings and cost of employees. Such reports are standard in the private sector for management. This practice would allow taxpayers and board members to become more aware of the actual costs.
